fatal_errors: The proposed dominant Al–Ti nonprotective scale contradicts the observed governing role of a continuous protective Cr-rich, primarily Cr2O3, layer.
The key controlled intervention—comparison of as-printed material with material aged at 750°C for 50 h to form L12/L21 precipitates—is omitted.
The hypothesis invents an oxidizing-versus-reducing atmosphere comparison even though the target study did not report such a comparison and did not explicitly specify its oxidation atmosphere.
It misses the central mediator: Cr depletion in aged precipitates and added matrix–precipitate interfaces delay protective Cr2O3 formation and increase oxidation.
Predicted spallation, interfacial-stress-driven cracking, and fatigue degradation are not supported by the reported oxidation results.
explanation: The response addresses high-temperature gas exposure and proposes measurable oxide-scale analyses, but it reconstructs neither the study design nor its central mechanism. The actual discriminating comparison was as-printed versus precipitation-aged alloy, not air versus H2–Ar. Aging generated Ni/Ti-rich L12 and Al/Ti-rich, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates; this redistributed Cr and introduced interfaces that delayed formation of the protective Cr2O3 scale. Consequently, the aged state gained more mass, especially at higher temperature, while both states retained similar activation energies and broadly Cr2O3-mediated protection. The generated hypothesis instead assigns control to rapid Al/Ti oxidation, poor adhesion, spallation, and stress-induced fatigue damage without supporting evidence. Its baseline captures the fcc cellular AM structure only generally, and its experiment is internally testable, but the conjunctive falsification rule is weak because failure to observe any one predicted feature would not necessarily falsify the full mechanism. No prior evidence is cited, and the proposed exposure boundaries do not reflect the observed transition around 900°C or the 600–1200°C, up-to-96-h study window.
